reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The whole profile hinges on a contact-power disconnect that shouldn't work this well, but it does. His xwOBA sits at .359 and his Hard-Hit rate at 48.8%, both in the upper tier, while his xBA lands at just .251, because a 34.0% chase rate creates enough swing-and-miss to suppress contact quality even when the batted balls are loud. What saves him is a 11.9% walk rate and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed that together paper over the strikeout number and turn singles that die for others into something more. If the chase rate ever tightens, he's a genuine star; if it doesn't, the projection's .272/.365/.517 line with 34 home runs and 39 steals still lands as one of the more complete offensive profiles in the National League.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .408 xwOBA and a 2.72 xERA on the same Statcast card is the whole argument. The contact quality against him is elite: hitters are barreling him at just 3.8% and making hard contact only 33.8% of the time, which is the floor that makes his strikeout rate sustainable even without a dominant chase number. On the hitting side, the 16.6% barrel rate and 93.4 mph average exit velocity say the projection's .935 OPS and 38 projected home runs are a fair read on what he does when healthy, with a 13.5% walk rate keeping the .389 OBP honest against a 23.0% strikeout rate that is the one real blemish in the profile. The dependency is innings: a full two-way workload at 32 is an ask that no comparables make easy, and if the pitching side gets managed back, you're left with a DH who is still one of the most dangerous bats in the league.

reports.name: James Wood

Wood also runs a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitter at this level can match. The whole thing hinges on whether a 28.6% strikeout rate, bottom 12% of the league, ever comes down, because at the current whiff rate the gap between what he should hit and what he actually hits stays wide. If it does compress even modestly, you're talking about a legitimate MVP-caliber season out of a 23-year-old; if it doesn't, the .387 OBP and the power still make him a middle-of-the-order force, just a noisier one.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The barrel rate carries this profile: 13.8% puts Stewart in rarified contact quality territory, and the .472 xSLG backs it up directly. What makes the power case interesting is the gap between average exit velocity (90.2 mph, comfortably above the median but not elite) and the barrel rate itself, he finds the sweetspot at a frequency that outpaces how hard he swings, which is a real swing quality story. The 10.1% walk rate keeps the .335 OBP honest given an xBA sitting right at the league midpoint, and a 21.9% strikeout rate that isn't a problem yet could become one if pitchers learn to exploit the 29.4% chase. At 22, with 34 projected home runs and 15 stolen bases across 692 projected plate appearances, he looks like a corner bat with genuine middle-of-the-order upside, unless the contact metrics stagnate and the xBA tells more than the barrel rate does.

His .468 xSLG and 47.4% hard-hit rate say genuine middle-of-the-order power, but a 36.8% chase rate drags his walk rate to 6.3% and keeps the projection at .299 OBP, which is what happens when a talented bat sells out in the zone. The swing-for-damage approach checks out: 11.5% barrels, 90.5 mph average exit velo, real pop. If the chase rate ever softens, even modestly, the .725 projected OPS has room to climb into something that looks like a true corner-of-the-lineup piece; if it doesn't, 25 home runs and 28 stolen bases from an outfielder who fields at the 86th percentile is still a useful player, just one the box score flatters less than the batted-ball data.

reports.name: Kevin McGonigle
reports.published_report: The .349 xwOBA is the number that explains everything else: it's built almost entirely on elite plate discipline rather than raw power, and that's an unusual foundation to trust. McGonigle's 19.0% chase rate sits at the 98th percentile, his 14.1% walk rate is similarly elite, and he makes enough contact that a 13.9% strikeout rate completes the picture of a hitter who genuinely controls the strike zone. The exit velocity profile, 87.9 mph average and 36.7% hard-hit, is below-average, so the .419 xSLG owes more to contact skill and approach than to brute force, and if pitchers eventually find a way to suppress his in-zone damage, the power ceiling compresses fast. reports.name: Andy Pages

What holds the profile together is plate discipline: a 32.1% chase rate is genuinely good, the strikeout rate sits at 19.8%, and that combination is what lets the contact translate instead of evaporating against better stuff. The projection fills out as a 26-homer, 15-steal outfielder with a .269/.333/.457 line across 679 plate appearances, a legitimate everyday regular, and the only real dependency is whether that walk rate, currently 8.2%, creeps up enough to sharpen the on-base side as pitchers adjust.

reports.name: Michael Harris II
reports.published_report: The .291 xBA sitting at the 97th percentile tells you the contact quality is legitimate, but the 3.9% walk rate is the number that keeps this profile from being what it should be. The problem is everything surrounding contact quality — a 40.4% chase rate and 35.8% whiff rate both grade near the bottom of the league, and a 33.0% K% lands at the 2nd percentile, which means pitchers have already found the answer on him. His .231 xBA tells you the strikeouts aren't all productive noise; he's genuinely missing too many hittable pitches for the batting average to hold up. If Coors keeps inflating the surface line and he sees enough left-handers he can turn on, there's a real slugging catcher here; if pitchers continue to exploit the chase issues with regularity, the strikeout rate swallows the counting stats and what's left is a boom-or-bust masher on a bad team.

reports.name: Pete Alonso
reports.published_report: The contact quality here is almost absurdly loud: 94.2 mph average exit velocity and a 56.3% hard-hit rate both sit at the 98th percentile, and a .386 xwOBA suggests the current batting average tells a flatter story than the underlying contact deserves. The projection's .258/.351/.481 with 35 home runs is the conservative translation of a Statcast profile that keeps insisting he hits the ball as hard as almost anyone in the league. The whole thing hinges on strikeouts, a 24.4% K% that's already a drag and gets more costly as he ages into his early thirties without the sprint speed (25.3 ft/s) to manufacture anything on the bases when he doesn't drive it out. If the strikeout rate creeps up and the hard contact stays, he's a true-outcome slugger posting somewhere well south of that .258 projection; if the contact rate firms up even modestly, the .533 xSLG is telling you a .481-plus SLG is legitimate and you're looking at a middle-of-the-order force for another few years.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .422 xwOBA tells you almost everything you need to know, and the 19.8% chase rate tells you why it's sustainable. Soto's contact quality sits at the very top of the league, with an xSLG of .589 and a barrel rate of 14.3%, while his 17.5% walk rate keeps pitchers from ever getting comfortable attacking him. The projection's .410 OBP and .948 OPS across 489 PA aren't optimistic; they're just what happens when a hitter with this chase profile and this much raw contact quality stays healthy. Sprint speed at 25.9 ft/s is a real limitation, so the ceiling here is defined entirely by the bat, and the bat is about as clean a profile as you'll find.

reports.name: Hagen Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the argument: 13.4 K/9 at AAA, which translates to 10.3 at the MLB level while the league sits at 8.6. The control is the counter-argument: 40 walks in 58.3 innings, a 6.2 BB/9 that translates to 5.0, and that's where the whole profile hangs. His K-BB% sits at 83rd percentile in the AAA pitcher pool because the swing-and-miss is loud enough to survive the walk rate for now, but a 19% K-BB% with a 1.4 WHIP is a profile that needs the strikeouts to stay elite, because the walks can't shrink without them. If the stuff translates and the command tightens even a little, he's a rotation piece; if the walks follow him to the big leagues at that rate, 58.3 innings of depth work is the ceiling.

reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The barrel rate and the strikeout rate live in opposite ends of the same profile, and that tension is the whole read on Neto. His 11.9% barrel rate is legitimate pop for a shortstop, but a 33.6% whiff rate and a 37.1% chase rate produce the kind of contact suppression that makes an .198 xBA believable — and the projection's .226 AVG is already banking on some positive regression there. If the chase rate doesn't come down, the 26 projected home runs become harder to reach because at-bats that end early on bad pitches can't become barrels.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing keeping this profile from being clean. García's xBA sits at .285 and his xSLG at .499, contact and power metrics that describe a genuine middle-of-the-order hitter, and a 12.3% barrel rate backs up the damage. The problem is a 39.0% chase rate and a 4.4% walk rate that together describe a hitter who will hand pitchers a way out. He makes enough contact when he swings, as a 19.2% whiff rate confirms, so the strikeouts aren't the crisis; the walks are, because they cap the ceiling on an otherwise imposing offensive profile. If pitchers learn to exploit the aggression more consistently, the .309 OBP in the projection holds and the power plays; if they punish it, the .841 OPS is aspirational.

reports.name: Luis Lara
reports.published_report: The contact and patience are loud: a .432 OBP at AAA, 54 walks against 48 strikeouts in 346 plate appearances, and a K% that translates to 17.6% at the MLB level while the average big-leaguer strikes out at 22.0%. Lara hits for average and gets on base at an elite clip, and the 24 stolen bases give him a real center-field offensive profile. The translation is honest about what he isn't, though: a .130 MLB-equivalent ISO tells you the game-to-game impact depends on contact and speed, not power, and if the BABIP softens when he faces better pitching, the ceiling lands closer to a low-end everyday regular than anything beyond it. That's the profile — a CF who earns his at-bats with a strike-zone approach that would play up immediately, but whose ceiling is ultimately capped by what the bat does when contact rates normalize.

reports.name: Alec Burleson
reports.published_report: The xBA and xSLG both sit at the 98th percentile, and a .283/.349/.475 projection doesn't fully close that gap. Burleson chases at a 37.0% rate, which is a real problem, but pitchers who test him in the zone pay for it — 92.0 mph average exit velocity, 49.6% hard-hit rate, a 16.4% strikeout rate that shows the contact holds even with the aggressive approach. The profile hinges on whether pitchers keep selling him chase looks outside the zone or start attacking him with strikes, because if they figure out the discipline isn't coming, the xSLG ceiling gets chipped away in a hurry. He's a first-division bat if the barrel keeps showing up, a flawed-but-useful run producer if the chase rate gets exploited more systematically.

reports.name: Ben Rice
reports.published_report: 41 projected home runs from a first baseman whose barrel rate sits at 15.1% is the kind of power that earns the number rather than outrunning it. The Statcast profile is lopsided in an interesting way: the contact quality metrics cluster in the 89th-to-94th percentile range while the swing-and-miss side of the ledger is genuinely problematic, with a 25.0% strikeout rate and a whiff rate that lands in the 39th percentile. What saves the profile is a 12.2% walk rate that keeps the .345 OBP afloat even when the bat misses, so the question isn't whether the power translates but whether pitchers can widen the zone on him and turn that K% ugly. If they can't, a .867 OPS first baseman who runs out 99 RBI is a lineup anchor; if they can, this becomes a high-variance slugger you roster for the home runs and tolerate everything else.

reports.name: Tarik Skubal
reports.published_report: That 4.3 BB% sits at the 99th percentile, and that's the spine of the whole profile. Skubal doesn't beat hitters by overwhelming contact quality, his Barrel% is dead average, but a 30.5 K% paired with that walk rate means he almost never gives innings away, and a .270 xwOBA confirms hitters just aren't doing damage when they do make contact. The projection calls for a 2.96 ERA over 151 innings, which tracks cleanly against a 3.01 xERA; the gap between those numbers is noise, not luck. The one genuine dependency is health: 151 projected innings is a real workload, and if he can't stay on the mound in Los Angeles, everything downstream shrinks with it.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the problem. At 38.5%, Lile is expanding the zone at a rate that lands in the 8th percentile, and his 5.6% walk rate follows directly from that — not from pitchers attacking the strike zone but from him leaving it voluntarily. The underlying contact quality is decent enough: an .422 xSLG and 8.5% barrel rate suggest real gap-to-gap pop, and his 29.3 ft/s sprint speed at the 93rd percentile gives the 16 projected stolen bases a genuine foundation. But a .301 OBP on 650 plate appearances is what happens when a young hitter with functional bat speed refuses to take a free pass, and the projection's .719 OPS reflects a profile that plays like a second-division regular until he learns to lay off pitches he can't do damage on. If the discipline develops, the speed and the power give him a real offensive floor to build from; if it doesn't, he's a stolen-base source with too many empty at-bats.

At 15.7%, he makes contact as cleanly as almost anyone, yet his average exit velocity is 86.0 mph, sitting at the 9th percentile — the bat finds the ball, but the ball doesn't go far. That gap is why xSLG lands at .371 despite a 9.3% walk rate keeping his xwOBA at a perfectly league-average .320, and it's what the 22-home-run projection hinges on: he has to keep elevating to manufacture power that soft contact doesn't naturally produce. If the launch profile regresses, what's left is a .347 OBP hitter who grounds into a lot of outs.

reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is quietly damning: a .288 xwOBA and a 28.6% hard-hit rate that both sit in the bottom tenth of the league, which makes the 25 projected home runs in the projection the one number that needs explaining. It gets explained, partly, by contact quality that plays up in the air — his 21.0% whiff rate and 14.2% strikeout rate say he puts the ball in play consistently enough to let the pull-side power show up without elite exit velocity behind it. The projection's .255/.312/.427 line is a second-division regular's season, useful in a lineup that doesn't need him to carry anything. The whole profile hinges on his strikeout discipline holding, because if that 14.2% K rate creeps toward league average, the below-average contact quality has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Payton Tolle
reports.published_report: The 36.1% chase rate is the engine here, and when hitters won't swing at your stuff out of the zone, the strikeout and contact-suppression numbers downstream tend to follow. Tolle's xwOBA of .257 and xERA of 2.72 both sit at the 94th percentile, and the 27.8% strikeout rate does real work without needing elite swing-and-miss; he's getting hitters to expand rather than blow them away in the zone. A 3.18 ERA over 154.0 projected innings with a 1.10 WHIP is the conservative translation of a profile that, by the underlying contact data, is pitching better than that. If the chase rate erodes and hitters stop biting, the 27.5% whiff rate doesn't have enough margin to carry the strikeout and contact numbers on its own.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 37.3% chase rate sits at the 97th percentile, and it's the load-bearing wall for everything else in his profile. Sánchez doesn't miss bats through velocity or spin — his 32.9% whiff rate and 28.0% strikeout rate are built almost entirely on hitters chasing, which means his 5.4% walk rate isn't just a number, it's proof that the zone control and the chase rate are working together. The contact quality is ordinary when hitters do connect, 42.1% hard-hit at the 22nd percentile, so the formula depends on keeping them uncomfortable enough to swing at bad pitches. If his ability to generate that chase deteriorates, a 3.32 xERA becomes a more honest ceiling than a floor, and the projection's 2.63 ERA with 231 strikeouts across 203.4 innings gets a lot harder to believe.

reports.name: Gavin Williams
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate and the hard-hit rate are telling opposite stories, and figuring out which one wins is the whole argument. Williams punches out 31.8% of hitters he faces, a genuinely elite mark, and his 31.2% whiff rate and 34.0% chase rate confirm the swing-and-miss is earned. But when contact lands, it lands hard: a 47.6% hard-hit rate and 11.7% barrel rate that sit at the bottom of the league, which is why his xERA sits at 3.89 despite all that swing-and-miss. The profile hinges on whether the strikeout volume keeps the damage from accumulating, and at 192.2 projected innings with 240 strikeouts and a 1.12 WHIP, ValuCast thinks it mostly does, arriving at a 3.74 ERA that's a touch friendlier than Statcast's contact picture alone would suggest. He's a genuine mid-rotation arm with top-of-rotation punch in his strikeout profile, carrying the caveat that a bad stretch of contact luck can make the surface results look much uglier than his stuff deserves.

reports.name: Brandon Marsh
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the anchor of the whole argument. At 37.4%, Marsh is swinging at pitches well outside the zone far more often than most hitters, and a 6.0% walk rate is the predictable result. What saves him is that when he does make contact, the ball goes — 45.7% hard-hit rate, an xBA that translates to .263, and enough pop that the projection lands at 20 home runs across a full season. The profile is essentially a hard-contact masher who gives away at-bats by chasing, which caps the OBP ceiling and keeps that .314 xwOBA stuck in ordinary territory despite the quality of his best swings. If the chase rate doesn't come down, he's a useful everyday corner outfielder with a floor that looks a lot like what you already see here.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is the cautionary note here. A 4.11 xERA and .313 xwOBA sit right at the league median, the strikeout rate at 22.2% is ordinary, and the 8.6% walk rate is a quiet drag on an arsenal that hasn't been limiting contact the way it once did. What's still working is the 27.0% whiff rate and a 31.7% chase rate, both comfortably above average, which tells you the stuff can still miss bats when it's on, and the 95.6 mph fastball keeps him from being purely a junk profile. The 3.26 ERA projection is doing real work to close the gap between what the peripherals suggest and what the final line might say, and 136.2 projected innings already builds in some return-from-injury caution. If the whiff and chase numbers are the real floor and his command tightens, he's a useful mid-rotation piece; if the contact numbers stay soft and the walks don't come down, you're looking at a league-average arm on an innings budget.

The power, though, is a different story: his .120 ISO at AAA translates to .114 in the majors, well short of the .150 MLB average, and a .199 average sitting on a .259 BABIP suggests the contact isn't beating defenders when it lands. Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

The projection at .223/.301/.406 with 21 home runs across a full season is essentially what he is right now: a catcher who can hurt you when he connects but who strikes out 29.4% of the time and leaves most of his raw pop on the floor. If the whiff rate ever gets tamed, the power and walk rate make him a useful everyday catcher; if it doesn't, he's a low-end regular whose value lives entirely at the position.

reports.name: Rafael Devers

The projection trusts the power to survive the strikeout load, and 31 home runs across a full 680 PA season would be a fair translation of the exit-velocity profile, with a 10.1% walk rate keeping the .325 OBP from collapsing under the 26.6% strikeout rate. reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The .389 xwOBA tells you most of what you need to know about where Harper sits among hitters right now. A 16.3% walk rate at the 98th percentile is doing a lot of heavy lifting: his 30.3% whiff rate and 33.2% chase rate are below-average marks that would hollow out a lesser hitter, but the elite plate discipline keeps pitchers from burying him, and the .502 xSLG says the power translates when he makes contact. The projection, .256/.372/.492 with 32 home runs across 683 plate appearances, flows directly from that profile: a mediocre batting average propped up by an OBP that most hitters can't approach, and enough slug to make the whole line dangerous. The one real dependency is that walk rate; if pitchers ever find a way to attack him more aggressively without paying, the contact metrics don't have enough margin to hold the line alone.

Rodriguez doesn't miss bats at an elite rate, his K% is 25.9% and his walk rate at 7.5% is functional rather than a weapon, so the whole thing runs on contact suppression, which his Statcast numbers say is genuine and repeatable. The 98.3 mph fastball gives hitters something to fear even when he's not blowing them away, and the 1.11 WHIP projection over 70.7 innings suggests the stuff translates to real outs. If the barrel suppression regresses toward ordinary, the strikeout profile isn't deep enough to carry him, but right now there's a strong case he's one of the better high-leverage options in San Diego's bullpen.

reports.name: Chase Petty
reports.published_report: The 6.70 ERA at AAA is the number that sets the table, and the translation doesn't soften it. Across 46 innings at AAA this season, Petty's 22 walks have pushed his BB/9 to 4.3, and when that number translates to a 3.9 at the MLB level, it's still walking more batters than a typical big-league arm does. His strikeouts are real enough, 46 of them at a 9.0 K/9, but a translated K-BB% of 11.4 against a pool where 13.5 is the baseline means he's threading a needle with fraying thread. If the walk rate tightens, there's a functional back-end arm in here; if it doesn't, depth piece is both the ceiling and the floor.

reports.name: Austin Riley
reports.published_report: The contact has fallen off a cliff. Riley's 32.8% whiff rate and 30.9% K% sit at the very bottom of the percentile distribution, and his xBA of .213 shows the strikeouts are doing real damage to the batting line. What makes this profile uncomfortable rather than simply bad is the power underneath it: a 12.5% barrel rate and 91.2 mph average exit velocity both grade in the 83rd percentile, and his .402 xSLG says the bat still has teeth when it connects. The ValuCast projection has him at .228/.300/.385 across 632 PA, a below-average regular whose 21 projected home runs keep him just relevant enough to hold a lineup spot, and the whole thing hinges on whether he can trim the whiff rate enough to let the barrel quality breathe.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The tension is simple: he makes excellent contact decisions but the ball doesn't always leave his bat with authority. Suzuki's 22.8% chase rate sits in the 88th percentile, and he converts that discipline into an 11.7% walk rate, which is how a .252 xBA becomes a .338 xwOBA — the plate approach is doing real work. What he isn't is a pure masher; 89.0 mph average exit velocity lands in the 44th percentile, and the 10.5% barrel rate earns its keep not through raw force but through consistent contact quality. The projection lands at 27 home runs and an .833 OPS across 615 plate appearances, which looks about right for a player whose ceiling is a quietly excellent middle-of-the-order piece, and whose floor, if the strikeout rate ticks up without the walk rate holding, is a useful but ordinary corner bat.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report: The whiff rate is loud and the fastball is louder, but the contact quality tells a different story. Sasaki's 29.7% whiff rate and 97.8 mph heater are legitimate weapons, yet hitters who do connect are squaring him up at a 44.4% hard-hit rate and a 10.2% barrel rate that both sit near the bottom of the league, and that gap between swing-and-miss ability and contact suppression is exactly why a 4.29 xERA tracks closer to back-end starter than frontline arm. The 9.6% walk rate is the profile's pressure point: if he can't pull that down in his first full MLB season, the strikeouts don't compensate enough to keep the damage manageable, and 145.2 projected innings at a 1.3 WHIP is a serviceable mid-rotation piece, not the ace the Dodgers imported.

He's fast enough (28.6 ft/s) to manufacture a little, and the projection credits him with 9 steals across 441 PA, but a 5.5% walk rate against that chase rate means he's making a lot of contact on pitches he probably shouldn't be chasing, which is a different thing than being a disciplined hitter. If the speed plays in the field and his bat-to-ball skill keeps him in lineups against tougher arms, he profiles as a useful utility piece; if the power floor holds where Statcast currently sees it, the .711 OPS projection is probably his ceiling, not a conservative floor.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Robby Snelling
reports.published_report: A 1.90 ERA and a 0.90 WHIP across 29 AAA innings would be the whole conversation if Snelling weren't sitting on the 60-day IL right now. His K-BB% at AAA ranks 97th in the pitcher pool, and the strikeout rate translates to 9.9 per nine at the MLB level, well clear of the MLB average of 8.6. The walk rate is the one honest wrinkle: 15 free passes in 29 AAA innings translates to 3.8 per nine in the majors, a little loose for a rotation piece, and that's what the floor hinges on. If the IL stint is short and the command firms up, he's more than a depth arm; if the walks don't tighten, that depth ceiling is probably where he lands.

reports.name: Ike Irish
reports.published_report: The .916 OPS across 343 A+ plate appearances is loud, and so is the .241 ISO. Ike Irish is hitting 16 home runs and stealing 20 bases while drawing 43 walks against 75 strikeouts, a profile that earns attention even at this level. The translation is where the story gets complicated: an MLB-equivalent K% of 25.4 is above league average, suggesting the swing-and-miss doesn't disappear when the stuff gets better, and the ISO translates to .159, essentially average power once you strip the level away. If the contact quality holds and the strikeout rate doesn't climb, he's a low-end regular; if the translation is what it looks like, he's a bench bat with pop.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Ty Southisene
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combo is genuinely loud for a 20-year-old; the power isn't. Across A+ & A in 2026, Ty Southisene is hitting .302 with a 12% strikeout rate, and his 45 walks against 42 strikeouts in 351 plate appearances is the kind of ratio you don't often see this young. That plate discipline translates to a 9.7% walk rate and 17.7% strikeout rate at the MLB level, both better than what most big leaguers manage, but the .081 ISO tells you the rest: an MLB-equivalent .088 ISO is thin, and 34 stolen bases can carry a profile only so far if that gap never closes. If the bat speed develops and the power follows, he's a useful regular who reaches base at a premium rate; if it doesn't, he's a bench piece whose elite contact plays in a limited role.

reports.name: Zac Thornton
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the thing to watch here. Across AAA & AA this season, Thornton has posted a 3.9 BB/9 over 62.7 innings, and when that translates to an MLB context it edges up to 3.7 while the league runs closer to 3.2. His strikeout translation lands at 8.3 K/9, just a tick below the MLB mean, which means the margin for error with runners on base is thin. The 4.0 ERA and 1.4 WHIP across AAA & AA aren't disqualifying, but the K-BB% translates to 12.0 where the league average sits at 13.5, so the profile reads as someone whose control needs to sharpen before the command catches up to the stuff. Left-handed depth arms can find roster spots on shape alone, but if the walk rate doesn't come down, that's the ceiling too.
